title: Example
body_md:
Using measurings, we are also able to define a more flexible version of the $\mathtt{map}$ function.
    Traditionally, $\mathtt{map}$ takes a function $f$ and a list and applies $f$ to all elements of the list element wise.
    Using measurings, we can actually specify a list of functions which gets applied to elements of a list in a pairwise fashion.
    For each $m \in M$, define the function $r_m \colon M \to M$ which multiplies an element of $M$ by $m$ from the right.
    We define the algebra
    \begin{align*}
        1+ M \times [M,M]^{\leq \infty} &\longrightarrow [M,M]^{\leq \infty}\\
        * &\longmapsto r_e\\
        (m,\ell) &\longmapsto r_m : \ell.
    \end{align*}
    We can now define the measuring
    \begin{align*}
        \varphi \colon {M^*}^\circ \times  [M,M]^{\leq \infty} &\to M^* \\
        ([\:], \ell) &\mapsto [\:]\\
        (\ell, [\:]) &\mapsto [\:]\\
        (m:\ell, f:k) &\mapsto f(m):\varphi(\ell, k).
    \end{align*}
    We verify this is a measuring by checking
    $
    \varphi(m':\ell, r_{m}:k) = r_{m}(m'):\varphi(\ell, k) = (m'\bullet m) :\varphi(\ell,k).
    $
    Note that we really need to define an algebra structure on $[M,M]^{\leq \infty}$ instead of a coalgebra structure, since there is no obvious way to extract $m \in M$ from a function $f \colon M \to M$ in such a way that the conditions on a measuring are satisfied.

title: Example
body_md:
For similar reasons as in \cref{ex:meauringtoX^*}, we remark there does not exist an algebra morphism $T_{M,n} \to T_M$.
    There does however exist a measuring from $T_{M,n}$ to $T_M$ by $T_{M,n}^\circ$.
    It is given by
    \begin{align*}
        \varphi\colon T_{M,n}^\circ \times T_{M,n} &\to T_{M} \\
        (e_T, (m,\ell, r)) &\mapsto e_T\\
        ((m',\ell', r'), e_T) &\mapsto e_T\\
        ((m',\ell',r') , (m,\ell, r)) &\mapsto y (m' \bullet m,\varphi(\ell', \ell), \varphi(r',r)),
    \end{align*}
    which is a measuring by definition.
    Again, for reasons similar to those seen in \cref{ex:meauringtoX^*} a measuring to $T_M$ does exist, where an algebra morphism does not.
    The coalgebra $T_{M,n}^\circ$ gives us control over which parts of an element in $T_{M,n}$ we consider.

title: Example
body_md:
If we only care about modifying the shape of an element in $T_M$ and don't want to introduce any twist, we can consider the measuring
    \begin{align*}
        \varphi \colon T_{\{e\}}^\circ \times T_M &\to T_M \\
        (e_T, (m,\ell, r)) &\mapsto e_T\\
        ((e,\ell', r'), e_T) &\mapsto e_T\\
        ((e,\ell',r') , (m,\ell, r)) &\mapsto y (m,\varphi(\ell', \ell), \varphi(r',r)),
    \end{align*}
    which is a measuring by definition.
    This measuring takes a tree containing only the unit of the monoid $t' \in T_{\{e\}}^\circ$ and uses its shape to modify a tree $t \in T_M$ to fit within the shape of $t'$.

title: Example
body_md:
Again, we can generalize the map function using a measuring to obtain more fine grained control over which function gets applied to which elements.
    Recall we define the function $r_m\colon M \to M$ as multiplication by $m$ on the right.
    Let $[M,M]$ be the set of functions $M \to M$, and let $T_{[M,M]}$ be the set of all binary trees with labels in $[M,M]$.
    We can then define an algebra structure on $T_{[M,M]}$ by
    \begin{align*}
        1 + M \times T_{[M,M]} \times T_{[M,M]} &\to T_{[M,M]} \\
        * &\mapsto e_T\\
        (m,\ell,r) &\mapsto (r_m, \ell, r).
    \end{align*}
    Now we have a measuring given by
    \begin{align*}
        \varphi\colon T_M^\circ \times T_{[M,M]} &\to T_M \\
        (e_T, (f, \ell, r)) &\mapsto e_T\\
        ((m', \ell', r'), e_T) &\mapsto e_T\\
        ((m', \ell', r'), (f, \ell, r)) &\mapsto (f(m), \varphi(\ell',\ell), \varphi(r',r)).
    \end{align*}
    To check this is a measuring, we verify
    $$
    \varphi((m', \ell', r'), (r_m, \ell, r)) =  (r_m(m'), \varphi(\ell',\ell), \varphi(r',r)) =  (m' \bullet m, \varphi(\ell',\ell), \varphi(r',r)).
    $$

title: Example
body_md:
For similar reasons as in previous examples, we remark there does not exist an algebra morphism $S_{M,n} \to S_M$.
    There does however exist a measuring from $S_{M,n}$ to $S_M$ by $S_{M,n}^\circ$.
    It is given by
    \begin{align*}
        \varphi\colon S_{M,n}^\circ \times S_{M,n} &\to S_{M} \\
        (e_S, (m,\ell)) &\mapsto e_S\\
        ((m',\ell'), e_T) &\mapsto e_T\\
        ((m',\ell') , (m,\ell)) &\mapsto (m' \bullet m,\,\mathtt{map}(\varphi)(\mathtt{zip}(\ell',\ell))),
    \end{align*}
    which is a measuring by definition.
    Again, reasoning similar to that seen in Example \ref{ex:meauringtoX^*} applies as to why a measuring to $S_M$ does exist, where an algebra morphism does not.
    The coalgebra $S_{M,n}^\circ$ gives us control over which parts of an element in $S_{M,n}$ we consider.

title: Lemma
body_md: Let $A$ be a $S_{M,n}^\circ$-initial algebra. Then $A$ is also $S_{M,n-1}^\circ$ initial.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Consider the coalgebra morphism $\iota\colon S_{M,n-1}^\circ \to S_{M,n}^\circ, s \mapsto s$.
    This induces a morphism
    \begin{align*}
        \iota\triangleright A \colon S_{M,n-1}^\circ \triangleright A &\to  S_{M,n}^\circ \triangleright A \\
        [e_{\operatorname{Fr}}] &\mapsto [e_{\operatorname{Fr}}]\\
        [s,a] &\mapsto [s,a]\\
        [m,\ell] &\mapsto [m, \mathtt{map}(\iota \triangleright A)(\ell)].
    \end{align*}
    This morphism is monomorphic by definition.
    Since $A$ is $S_{M,n}^\circ$-initial, we know $S_{M,n} \triangleright A$ is an initial object.
    This means $\iota\triangleright A $ is a monomorphism into the initial object, hence an isomorphism.
head: environment

title: Corollary
body_md: Let $A$ be a $S_{M,n}^\circ$-initial algebra. Then $A$ is also $S_{M,k}^\circ$ initial for all $k \leq n$.
head: environment

label: lem:adddepth
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:adddepth}
    Let $A$ be a $S_{M,n}^\circ$-initial algebra and let $\varphi\colon S_{M,n}^\circ \times A \to S_M$ be the unique measuring from $A$ to $S_{M}$ by $S_{M,n}^\circ$.
    For all $0 \leq i \leq n$, let  $s_i \in S_{M,n}$ be the largest tree of depth $i$ in $S_{M,n}$ which contains only the unit $e \in M$.
    Then for all $0 \leq i \in n$ and $0 \leq j \leq n-i$ we have
    $$
    \varphi_{s_i}(a) = \varphi_{s_i}( 
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{A}\circ\varphi_{s_{i+j}} (a)).
    $$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $k\leq n$.
    First, we define a function which takes two trees and appends the second tree to all the roots of the first tree.
    We define it as
    \begin{align*}
        (++) \colon S_{M,\infty} \times S_{M,\infty} &\to S_{M,\infty} \\
        (e_S, s) &\mapsto s\\
        ((m, \ell), s) &\mapsto (m, \mathtt{map}( (++) s )(\ell)).
    \end{align*}
    For all $0 \leq j \leq n-k$, define the coalgebra morphism
    \begin{align*}
        p_j\colon S_{M,k}^\circ &\to S_{M,n}^\circ \times S_{M,n}^\circ \\
        s &\mapsto (s,\widetilde{s} ++ s_j),
    \end{align*}
    where $\widetilde{s}$ is the unique tree $\widetilde{s} \in S_{\{e\}, k}$ such that $\mathtt{shape}(\widetilde{s}) = \mathtt{shape}(s)$.
                                              
    Consider the composition of measurings $\varphi \circ (\mathrm{id} \times  
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{A} \circ \varphi) \in \mu_{S_{M,n}^\circ \times S_{M,n}^\circ}(A,S_{M})$.
    We can precompose this measuring with the coalgebra morphism $p_j$ to obtain a measuring
    $$
    S_{M,k}^\circ \times A \xrightarrow{p_j \times \mathrm{id}_A} S_{M,n}^\circ \times S_{M,n}^\circ \times A \xrightarrow{\varphi \circ (\mathrm{id} \times  
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{A} \circ \varphi)} S_{M}.
    $$
               
    We also have the coalgebra morphism $\iota\colon S_{M,k}^\circ  \to S_{M,n}^\circ, s \mapsto s$ which we can precompose with $\varphi$.
    This gives us a measuring
    $$
    S_{M,k}^\circ \times A \xrightarrow{\iota \times \mathrm{id}_A} S_{M,n}^\circ \times A \xrightarrow{\varphi} S_{M}.
    $$  
    Since $A$ is also $S_{M,k}^\circ$-initial, we know these measurings must coincide.
    Hence we can state
    $
    \varphi(s,a) = \varphi(s, 
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{A} \circ \varphi(\widetilde{s} ++ s_j,a))
    $
    for all $s \in S_{M,k}^\circ$ and $0 \leq j \leq n-k$.
    The only restriction placed on $k$ was that $k \leq n$.
    Iterating over all $0 \leq k \leq n$, we arrive at the desired result
    $$
    \varphi(s,a) = \varphi(s, 
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{A}\circ \varphi(\widetilde{s} ++ s_j,a))
    $$
    for all $0 \leq i \leq n$ and $0 \leq j \leq n-i$.
    In particular this holds for $s = s_i$, and noting $s_i ++ s_j = s_{i + j}$ we obtain the desired result.
head: environment

label: cor:bound
title: Corollary
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We will proceed by induction over $i$.
    For the base case $i = 0$, we have $s_0 = e_S$, so $\varphi(s_0, a) = e_S \in S_{M,0}$.
    For the induction step, assume $\varphi(s_i, a) \in S_{M,i}$.
    Using $s_{i+1} = (e,(s_i)^{(\infty)})$ and the previous lemma we can write
    $
    \varphi(s_{i+1}, a) = \varphi( (e,(s_i)^{(\infty)}),  
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{A}(\varphi(s_{i+1}, a))).
    $
    Let $\alpha\colon 1 + M \times (S_M)^{\leq \infty} \to S_M$, then we can write $(m,s) = \alpha^{-1}(\varphi(s_{i+1}, a))$ where $s$ is the list with components $s_i$.
    We then know by definition of a measuring that
    $$
    \varphi(s_{i+1}, a)  = \varphi( (e,(s_i)^{(\infty)}),  
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{A}(\varphi(s_{i+1}, a))) = 
    (e \bullet m, \mathtt{map}(\varphi)(\mathtt{zip}((s_i)^{(\infty)}, k)   ) ),
    $$
    where $k = \mathtt{map}( 
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{A})(s)$.
    By the induction hypothesis, we know $$\mathtt{map}(\varphi)(\mathtt{zip}((s_i)^{(\infty)}, k)   )  \in (S_{M,i})^{\leq \infty},$$ hence $\varphi(s_{i+1}, a) \in S_{M,i + 1}$ by definition.
    This concludes the induction step and the proof.

title: Definition

title: Remark
body_md:
With this new definition, we can restate  \cref{lem:adddepth} as
    $$
    \varphi_i = \varphi_i \circ  
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{A} \circ \varphi_{i+j}
    $$
    for all $0 \leq i \leq n$ and $0 \leq j \leq n-i$.

label: prop:AtoS_nexists
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:AtoS_nexists}
    The functions $\varphi_k\colon A \to S_{M,k}$ from  \cref{def:AtoS_k} are algebra morphisms for all $0 \leq k \leq n$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We proceed by induction over $k$.
    For $k = 0$, we have that $S_{M,k} \cong 1$, the terminal object in $\mathrm{Set}$.
    Hence $\varphi_0\colon A \to S_{M,0}$ is an algebra morphism.
    For the inductive step, assume $\varphi_{k-1}\colon A \to S_{M,k-1}$ is an algebra morphism.
    We wish to show $\varphi_k$ is an algebra morphism.
    In more detail, we aim to show $$\alpha_k(m, \mathtt{map}(\varphi_k)(\ell)) = \varphi_k(\alpha(m,\ell))$$ for all $(m,\ell) \in M \times A^{\leq \infty}$.
    First, we will write $\ell = (a_i)_{i = 0}^j$, where $j \in {\mathbb N_\infty}$.
    We can now write
    \begin{align*}
        \alpha_k(m, \mathtt{map}(\varphi_k)(\ell))
        &= \alpha_k(m, \mathtt{map}(\varphi_k)((a_i)_i))\\
        &= \alpha_k(m, (\varphi_k(a_i))_i)\\
        &= \alpha_k(m, (\varphi_k \circ  
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{A} \circ \varphi_k(a_i))_i).
    \end{align*}
    Writing $\varphi_k \circ  
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{A} \circ \varphi_k(a_i) = t_i$, we can make the case distinction
    $$ 
    t_i = 
    \begin{cases}
        e_S &\text{ if } \varphi_k(a_i) = e_S \in S_M \\
        (m_i, \mathtt{map}(\varphi_{k-1} \circ  
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{A})(a_i)) &\text{ if } \varphi_k(a_i) = (m_i,a_i) \in S_M
    \end{cases}
    $$
    by $\varphi \colon S_{M,n}^\circ \times A \to S_M$ being a measuring.
    This means $$\alpha_k(m, \mathtt{map}(\varphi_k)(\ell)) = \alpha_k(m, (t_i)_i).$$
    By the algebra structure of $S_{M,k}$, we can write this as
    $
    \alpha_k(m, (t_i)_i) = (m,(r_i)_i),
    $
    where
    $$
    r_i = 
    \begin{cases}
        e_S &\text{ if } \varphi_k(a_i) = e_S \in S_M \\
        \alpha_{k-1}(m_i, \mathtt{map}(\varphi_{k-1} \circ  
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{A})(a_i)) &\text{ if } \varphi_k(a_i) = (m_i,a_i) \in S_M.
    \end{cases}
    $$
    By the induction hypothesis
    $
    \alpha_{k-1}(m_i, \mathtt{map}(\varphi_{k-1} \circ  
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{A})(a_i)) 
    = (\varphi_{k-1} \circ  
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{A})(m_i, a_i)
    $
    and we can write
    $$
    r_i = (\varphi_{k-1} \circ  
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{A})(\varphi_k(a_i)) = (\varphi_{k-1} \circ  
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{A} \circ \varphi_{k-1})(a_i)
    $$
    using \cref{lem:adddepth}.
    Retracing our steps, we now compute
    \begin{align*}
        \alpha_k(m, \mathtt{map}(\varphi_k)(\ell))
        &= (m,(r_i)_i)\\
        &= (m, (\varphi_{k-1} \circ  
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{A} \circ \varphi_{k-1})(a_i)_i)\\
        &= (m, \mathtt{map}(\varphi_{k-1}) (( 
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{A} \circ \varphi_{k-1})(a_i))_i)\\
        &= \varphi_k(\alpha(m,  ( 
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{A} \circ \varphi_{k-1})(a_i))_i  ))\\
        &= (\varphi_k \circ  
  \mathord{\mathpalette\raised@mathinvertedexclamationmark\relax} 
_{A} \circ \varphi_k)(\alpha(m, (a_i)_i ))\\
        &= \varphi_k(\alpha(m, \ell))
    \end{align*}
    using that $\varphi$ is a measuring twice.
    We conclude $\varphi_k \colon A \to S_{M,k}$ is an algebra morphism for all $0 \leq k \leq n$.

label: lem:AtoS_nunique
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:AtoS_nunique}
    For any $S_{M,n}^\circ$-initial algebra $A$, there exist at most one algebra morphism $A \to S_{M,n}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By \cref{prop:map from initial alg to dual}, there exists a unique morphism $A \to [S_{M,n}^\circ, S_{M}]$ for any $S_{M,n}^\circ$-initial algebra $A$.
    Since $S_{M,n}$ is $S_{M,n}^\circ$-initial we know there exists a unique morphism $\iota \colon S_{M,n} \rightarrowtail [S_{M,n}^\circ, S_{M}]$.
         
    This map is given by
    \begin{align*}
        \iota \colon S_{M,n} &\to [S_{M,n}^\circ, S_{M}] \\
        e_S &\mapsto \operatorname{const}_{e_S}\\
        (m,\ell) &\mapsto
        \left( 
        s' \mapsto 
        \begin{cases}
            e_S &\text{ if } s' = e_S \\
            (m'\bullet m, \mathtt{map}(\iota)(\mathtt{zip}(\ell,\ell'))) &\text{ if } s' = (m', \ell').
        \end{cases}
        \right).
    \end{align*}
    We can easily conclude $\iota$ is a monomorphism by observing that $\iota(s)(s_n) = s$ for all $s \in S_{M,n}$.
    Given any two morphisms $f,g\colon A \to S_{M,n}$, we can draw the following diagram
    \[\begin{tikzcd}
        A & {[S_{M,n}^\circ, S_{M}]} \\
        & S_{M,n}
        \arrow["{!}", from=1-1, to=1-2]
        \arrow["f"', shift right, from=1-1, to=2-2]
        \arrow["g", shift left, from=1-1, to=2-2]
        \arrow["\iota"', tail, from=2-2, to=1-2].
    \end{tikzcd}\]
    Since the morphism $A \to [S_{M,n}^\circ, S_{M}]$ is unique, we know the composites $\iota \circ f = \iota \circ g$, and by $\iota$ being mono we conclude $f = g$.
    Hence, there can be at most one algebra morphism from a $S_{M,n}^\circ$-initial algebra $A$ to $S_{M,n}$.
head: environment

title: Theorem
body_md: The algebra $S_{M,n}$ is the terminal $S_{M,n}^\circ$-initial algebra.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Given an $S_{M,n}^\circ$-initial algebra $A$, by  \cref{prop:AtoS_nexists}, we obtain an algebra morphism $\varphi_n \colon A \to S_{M,n}$.
    By \cref{lem:AtoS_nunique}, it is unique.
    We conclude $\mathbb{n}$ is the terminal $S_{M,n}^\circ$-initial algebra.
